Confirmed the transition from vapour-pressure-driven outward expulsion at low pressure to gas-entrainment-driven inward flow at atmospheric pressure. At 1 atm, denudation zone widths of several hundred µm on each side of the track were measured for 316L at 100–200 W, 0.1–1 m/s, with 50 µm powder layers.\\n\\n### Quantitative Denuded-Zone Widths\\n\\nThe denuded zone width (measured from the track edge to the boundary where undisturbed powder begins) depends on P, v, layer thickness, and ambient pressure. Representative values at 1 atm:\\n\\n- **316L, P ≈ 150–200 W, v ≈ 0.5–1.5 m/s, ~50 µm spot, ~30–50 µm layer, 1 atm Ar:** The total denuded zone (track + cleared region on both sides) is typically **2–5× the solidified track width**. For a track width of ~100–200 µm, the total powder-free zone extends ~300–800 µm. On each side, denudation extends roughly **100–400 µm** beyond the track edge (Matthews et al. 2016; Ly et al. 2017).\\n\\n- **At higher power or lower speed (approaching keyhole regime, P ≈ 300–400 W, v ≈ 0.3–0.8 m/s):** The vapour plume is more intense, entrainment stronger, and denudation zones widen. Total denuded widths can reach **0.5–1.0 mm** or more (Matthews et al. 2016).\\n\\n- **Ti-6Al-4V:** Similar or somewhat larger denudation widths than 316L at comparable energy inputs, due to lower boiling point of aluminium constituents and higher vapour pressures (Matthews et al. 2016).\\n\\n- **AlSi10Mg:** Denudation can be particularly wide due to the high vapour pressure of Mg and Al (Yin et al., 2020, *Additive Manufacturing* 31, 100958, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2019.100958).\\n\\n### Ratio of Denuded-Zone Width to Track Width\\n\\nThe ratio of total denuded-zone width (both sides combined) to the solidified bead width is typically **2–5×** at atmospheric pressure, meaning the denuded zone extends roughly **0.5–2× the track width** on each side beyond the bead edge. This ratio increases with increasing linear energy density (P/v) and is largest in keyhole-mode conditions where the vapour plume is most intense.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 2. How a Previously Fused Neighbour Changes the Next Track\\n\\n### Mechanisms of Interaction\\n\\nWhen a second track is placed within the denuded zone of the first, several effects alter the second track relative to a truly isolated single track:\\n\\n1. **Reduced or absent powder:** The neighbour\\\'s denudation has removed powder from the overlap region. The second track sees thinner or no powder on its near side, reducing the mass of material available for melting and altering the bead\\\'s cross-sectional geometry (asymmetric wetting, reduced height on the depleted side).\\n\\n2. **Raised solidified bead of the neighbour:** The first track\\\'s bead protrudes above the substrate surface (typically 10–40 µm for a single layer on a flat substrate). If the second track is close enough, the raised bead acts as a geometric obstacle, altering gas flow patterns and potentially deflecting the melt pool.\\n\\n3. **Pre-captured particles:** Particles that would have been available to the second track have already been drawn into the first track\\\'s melt pool or ejected as spatter.\\n\\n4. **Thermal pre-heating:** If the second track is exposed soon after the first and is nearby, residual heat in the substrate can modestly elevate the local temperature (see Section 4).\\n\\n### Experimental Evidence\\n\\n- **Yadroitsev et al. (2007, 2010, 2015)**: In systematic single-track and multi-track experiments on 316L and other alloys (e.g., *Journal of Materials Processing Technology* 210, 1624–1631, DOI: 10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2010.05.010), overlap studies showed that decreasing hatch spacing below about 60–70% of the single-track width led to degraded second-track geometry, increased porosity, and balling. At spacings below the denuded-zone width, the second track effectively scans on a partially bare substrate.\\n\\n- **Yadroitsev and Smurov (2010)** (*Physics Procedia* 5, 551–560, DOI: 10.1016/j.phpro.2010.08.083): Demonstrated that single-track stability maps (balling vs. continuous) change when neighbouring tracks are present, with the stable processing window narrowing for later tracks in a set.\\n\\n- **Mindt et al. (2016)** (*Metallurgical and Materials Transactions A* 47, 3811–3822, DOI: 10.1007/s11661-016-3470-2): Computational fluid dynamics simulations of multi-track powder bed melting showed asymmetric melt-pool shapes and altered penetration depth when a second track overlaps with a first track\\\'s denuded zone and solidified bead.\\n\\n### Implication for Isolated Single-Track Experiments\\n\\nTo ensure each track behaves as if alone on an undisturbed powder layer, the centre-to-centre spacing must exceed twice the one-sided denudation distance plus the half-widths of both tracks—i.e., the total denuded-zone width of each track must not overlap. A practical criterion is that the spacing must exceed the **total denuded-zone width** of a single track. Since this can be 2–5× the track width, spacings of **≥3× the expected melt-pool width** (or ≥1.5–2.5 mm for typical 316L conditions) are needed.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 3. Spatter and Ejecta: Travel Distance, Gas Flow, and Scan Direction\\n\\n### Spatter Travel Distance\\n\\nSpatter particles (molten or partially solidified droplets ejected from the melt pool or powder bed) can travel significant distances:\\n\\n- **Typical travel distances:** 1–20 mm from the track, with most spatter landing within **2–5 mm**. Large (>50 µm) spatter particles follow ballistic trajectories and land within a few mm; smaller particles can be carried farther by the gas flow (Ly et al. 2017; Gunenthiram et al., 2018, *Additive Manufacturing* 21, 517–528, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2018.02.003).\\n\\n- **Lutter-Günther et al. (2018)** and **Young et al. (2020)** (*Additive Manufacturing* 36, 101439, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2020.101439): Spatter can land >10 mm from the scan track when carried by the cross-flow gas, particularly downstream.\\n\\n### Gas Flow Velocity and Direction\\n\\n- In commercial L-PBF machines such as the Concept Laser M2, shielding gas (Ar or N₂) flows across the build plate at velocities of approximately **1–3 m/s** at the plate surface level. The gas enters from one side (inlet) and exits at the opposite side (outlet), carrying the vapour plume, condensate, and entrained spatter particles toward the outlet.\\n\\n- **Ladewig et al. (2016)** (*Additive Manufacturing* 12, 307–319, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2016.06.012): Showed that inadequate gas flow leads to condensate and spatter deposition on the powder bed, degrading subsequent track quality. Gas flow velocities of ≥1.5 m/s are needed to adequately remove the plume.\\n\\n- **Anwar and Pham (2017)** (*Rapid Prototyping Journal* 23, 631–647, DOI: 10.1108/RPJ-09-2015-0132) and **Ferrar et al. (2012)** (*Journal of Materials Processing Technology* 212, 355–364, DOI: 10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2011.09.020): Demonstrated position-dependent part quality related to gas flow non-uniformity across the build plate.\\n\\n### Exposure Order Relative to Gas Flow\\n\\nThe optimal strategy is to **expose tracks progressively from the gas-outlet (downstream) side toward the gas-inlet (upstream) side**. This ensures that spatter and condensate carried by the gas flow are deposited on regions where tracks have already been exposed, rather than contaminating powder reserved for later tracks.\\n\\n- **Anwar and Pham (2017)** and **Philo et al. (2019)** (*International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology* 105, 1025–1037): Confirmed that parts built on the downstream side of the build plate can show degraded surface quality due to spatter accumulation from upstream exposures.\\n\\n### Scan Direction Relative to Gas Flow\\n\\n- **Scanning into (against) the gas flow** is generally preferred: the plume is blown away from the advancing melt pool, minimizing beam attenuation by the vapour plume and condensate. The laser beam passes through cleaner gas before reaching the melt pool.\\n\\n- **Scanning with the gas flow** can cause the plume to linger over the melt pool or be carried ahead of the advancing beam, increasing beam attenuation and depositing condensate on upcoming powder.\\n\\n- **Scanning across the gas flow** is a reasonable compromise and is the geometry that naturally arises when tracks are perpendicular to the gas flow direction.\\n\\n- **Bidare et al. (2018)** and **Reijonen et al. (2020)** (*Additive Manufacturing* 33, 101120, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2020.101120): Demonstrated measurable effects of scan direction relative to gas flow on track quality and consistency.\\n\\n### Plume–Beam Interaction\\n\\nThe vapour plume attenuates and partially scatters the incident laser beam. At 1070 nm, the primary attenuation mechanism is scattering and absorption by condensed nano-particles in the plume, not absorption by the vapour itself. This attenuation depends on plume density, height, and the beam path through it—all of which depend on gas flow velocity and the scan direction relative to the flow (Bidare et al. 2018; Ly et al. 2017).\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 4. Thermal Effects from Neighbouring Tracks\\n\\n### Substrate Temperature Rise\\n\\nFor a single-layer track on a thick (≫1 mm) metallic substrate, the thermal field decays rapidly both in time and laterally. The relevant thermal diffusivity of 316L is α ≈ 4–5 mm²/s at room temperature.\\n\\n- **Lateral thermal penetration:** The characteristic thermal diffusion length is √(4αt). After t = 0.1 s, the diffusion length is √(4 × 5 × 0.1) ≈ 1.4 mm. However, the peak temperature at this distance is already reduced by orders of magnitude from the melt-pool peak.\\n\\n- **Rosenthal solution estimates:** For a point source moving at v = 1 m/s on a semi-infinite 316L substrate with P = 200 W (absorbed power ~60–80 W), the quasi-steady-state temperature rise at a lateral distance of 1.5–2 mm from the track centreline is of order **1–10 °C** above the far-field substrate temperature. At 2.5 mm lateral distance, the rise is negligible (<1–2 °C).\\n\\n- **After the laser passes:** Once the heat source has moved away, the local temperature at a fixed point decays approximately as t⁻¹ (for a line-source approximation) or faster. Within ~0.1–1 s after the heat source passes, the substrate temperature at distances >1 mm is within a few degrees of ambient.\\n\\n### When Thermal Interaction Can Be Neglected\\n\\nFor **single-layer isolated tracks** separated by ≥1.5–2 mm on a thick substrate, and with even modest time delays (galvo repositioning, ~0.01–1 s), the thermal perturbation from one track at the location of its neighbour is negligible compared to the ~1400–1700 °C temperatures in the melt pool. The pre-heating effect is at most a few °C and does not meaningfully alter melt-pool dimensions or regime classification.\\n\\n**Exposure order and waiting time** are therefore **not critical for thermal reasons** in single-layer, well-separated tracks, but they remain important for **denudation, spatter, and gas-flow reasons** (Sections 2–3).\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 5. Published Single-Track Study Practices\\n\\n### Spacings, Track Lengths, and Tracks Per Substrate\\n\\n- **Yadroitsev et al. (various, 2007–2015):** Typically used track lengths of 10–20 mm, spacings of 1–3 mm, with 10–50+ tracks per substrate panel. Cross-sections taken perpendicular to the scan direction. Phenix PM100 system, 50–70 W Yb fibre laser, 70 µm spot, 316L and CoCr (Yadroitsev et al., *Journal of Materials Processing Technology* 210, 2010, DOI: 10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2010.05.010).\\n\\n- **Kamath et al. (2014), LLNL Concept Laser M2:** Single tracks in 316L at P = 150–400 W, v = 0.1–2.2 m/s, 30 µm layers. Tracks spaced ~2 mm apart, 10 mm long, with dozens of tracks per 80×80 mm substrate. Cross-sections polished and imaged by optical microscopy. (*Kamath et al., International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology* 74, 65–78, DOI: 10.1007/s00170-014-5954-9.)\\n\\n- **Johnson et al. / Karayagiz et al. (2019–2020):** Single tracks on Concept Laser M2, 316L, similar spacings (~2 mm), 10–15 mm lengths. Compared measurements with CALPHAD-informed simulations. (*Karayagiz et al., Acta Materialia* 185, 320–339, DOI: 10.1016/j.actamat.2019.12.014.)\\n\\n- **NIST AM Bench (2018, 2022):** Standardized single-track and multi-track experiments in bare-plate and single-layer configurations. Nickel alloy 625 and 316L. Tracks ~1 mm and 12 mm long, spaced ~1.25–4 mm apart. Full experimental details and data publicly available (Montgomery et al., *Integrating Materials and Manufacturing Innovation* 8, 2019, DOI: 10.1007/s40192-019-00155-y; Levine et al., *Integrating Materials and Manufacturing Innovation* 9, 2020, DOI: 10.1007/s40192-020-00195-5). AM Bench used ~0.8–1.25 mm spacing for closely studied multi-track pads and wider spacing for isolated single tracks.\\n\\n- **Aboulkhair et al. (2014):** Single tracks in AlSi10Mg, EOS M270, 195 W, 70 µm spot, 25 µm layer. Tracks ~10 mm long, several mm apart. (*Aboulkhair et al., Additive Manufacturing* 1–4, 77–86, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2014.08.001.)\\n\\n- **Ghasemi-Tabasi et al. (2020–2022):** Single tracks in various alloys, typically 10 mm length, ≥2 mm spacing. (*Ghasemi-Tabasi et al., Additive Manufacturing* 47, 102357, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2021.102357.)\\n\\n- **Weissbach & Hart (2024):** High-throughput single-track experiments, tracks ~10 mm long, ≥1–2 mm spacing, dozens per substrate panel, systematically varying P and v. (*Materials & Design*, 2024.)\\n\\n### Sectioning Constraints\\n\\nWhen sectioning multiple tracks in one transverse cut:\\n\\n- **Saw kerf:** A precision abrasive (Buehler IsoMet or similar) saw has a kerf of ~0.3–0.8 mm. This does not limit track spacing but does consume material.\\n- **Mount size:** Standard metallographic mounts are 25 mm or 30 mm diameter; a 32 mm mount can accommodate ~30 mm of sample width, fitting 12–15 tracks at 2 mm spacing.\\n- **SEM field of view:** Imaging individual tracks at high magnification (e.g., 200–500×) gives fields of ~0.2–0.6 mm; for overview imaging (50–100×), fields of ~1–2 mm. At 2 mm spacing, adjacent tracks are distinguishable in low-mag images, and each track can be individually imaged at high mag without the neighbour in the field.\\n- **Practical approach:** Section the 80 mm panel into 2–3 pieces (e.g., ~25–30 mm each) to fit standard mounts, grinding each to the same plane (5–8 mm from the track start). Polish and image all tracks in a piece sequentially.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 6. The Effective Powder Layer\\n\\n### Packing Fraction and Effective Thickness\\n\\nA single layer of gas-atomized 316L powder (15–45 µm, D50 ≈ 30 µm) spread by a rigid blade or rubber-lip recoater onto a flat substrate has:\\n\\n- **Apparent (tap) packing fraction:** ~50–65% of full density, depending on powder size distribution, morphology, spreading speed, and recoater type. The packing fraction of a single thin layer can be lower than the bulk tap density, particularly for layer thicknesses approaching the D90 of the powder.\\n\\n- **Effective solid-material thickness:** For a nominal layer thickness t_nom of 30–50 µm and packing fraction φ ≈ 0.5–0.6, the effective solid thickness is t_eff = φ × t_nom ≈ 15–30 µm. This is the thickness of fully dense material that contains the same mass as the powder layer.\\n\\n- **Spierings et al. (2011)** (*Rapid Prototyping Journal* 17, 195–202, DOI: 10.1108/13552541111124770) and **Jacob et al. (2018)** (*Additive Manufacturing* 22, 462–473, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2018.05.025): Characterized powder spreading and effective layer properties.\\n\\n### Substrate Flatness and Insert Height Offsets\\n\\n- If the substrate panel is recessed below the build plate surface (even by 10–20 µm), the first powder layer will be thicker than nominal, potentially substantially so. Conversely, a proud (raised) insert gives a thinner-than-nominal layer.\\n- A height offset δ adds directly to the effective layer: t_actual ≈ t_nom + δ. This is a first-order effect that can dominate the melt-pool geometry for thin layers.\\n- **Recommendation:** Measure panel flatness and height relative to the build plate with a dial indicator or coordinate measuring machine. Target ±5–10 µm or better.\\n\\n### How the Thermo-Calc AM Module and Similar Models Treat the Powder Layer\\n\\n- The **Thermo-Calc AM Module** (Scheil-based solidification with CALPHAD thermodynamics and a heat-source model) treats the powder layer as a **continuum** with modified thermal properties. The powder is modelled as a homogeneous layer of reduced thermal conductivity (typically 1–5% of the bulk conductivity) and reduced density (packing fraction × bulk density). The effective thickness and packing fraction are input parameters.\\n\\n- The **heat source** is applied to this effective medium, and the melt pool is computed in quasi-steady state. The absorptivity is typically a calibration parameter. The Gaussian or keyhole-mode heat source model is fitted to experimental cross-section data.\\n\\n- The **Eagar–Tsai model** (Eagar & Tsai, 1983, *Welding Journal* 62, 346s–355s) does **not** explicitly treat a powder layer: it assumes a semi-infinite homogeneous solid with a Gaussian surface heat source. When applied to L-PBF, the powder layer\\\'s effect is implicitly absorbed into the calibrated absorptivity and possibly into effective thermal properties. The model predicts melt-pool width and depth in the substrate but does not capture the bead height above the surface or the effect of powder feedstock.\\n\\n- More sophisticated models (e.g., Goldak double-ellipsoid, ALE3D, Flow-3D, COMSOL-based models) can explicitly model the powder layer as a porous medium or as discrete particles, but for the steady-state single-track cross-section comparisons envisioned here, the Thermo-Calc and Eagar–Tsai approaches require only the effective layer parameters as inputs.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Practical Recommendation Table\\n\\nThe following table summarizes the recommended experimental layout for isolated single-track experiments in 316L at the conditions specified (P = 50–400 W, v = 0.1–3 m/s, 30–50 µm nominal layer, 1 atm Ar or N₂, Concept Laser M2).\\n\\n<artifact id="artifact-00"/>\\n\\n### Key Scaling Relationships\\n\\n- **Denudation zone width ∝ (P/v)^n**, where n ≈ 0.3–0.5 (weakly supported quantitatively; the trend is well established but the exponent depends on the specific alloy, powder, and ambient conditions).\\n- **Melt-pool width ∝ (P/v)^0.3–0.5** in conduction mode (Eagar–Tsai scaling); wider in keyhole mode.\\n- **Minimum spacing ≈ total denuded-zone width ≈ 2–5 × track width.** Since track widths for 316L at these conditions range from ~80 µm (low P, high v) to ~400+ µm (high P, low v, keyhole), spacings of 1.5–2.5 mm cover the range with margin.\\n\\n### Summary of Confidence Levels\\n\\n- **Strongly supported:** The denudation mechanism (vapour-jet entrainment at 1 atm); the qualitative scaling of denudation with P/v; the downstream-to-upstream exposure strategy; the importance of controlling scan direction relative to gas flow; the effective powder layer being thinner than nominal.\\n- **Moderately supported:** Specific denudation zone widths (vary with machine, powder lot, layer thickness, and gas flow); exact thermal decay thresholds; optimal scan direction (into vs. across gas flow); packing fraction values for specific recoater/powder combinations.\\n- **Weakly supported:** Exact quantitative thresholds for when thermal interaction becomes significant for single-layer tracks; precise spatter landing distances for specific machines; the universality of specific spacing recommendations across different machine architectures.\\n\\n### References Summary (with DOIs)\\n\\n1. Matthews, M. J. et al. (2016). Denudation of metal powder layers in laser powder bed fusion processes. *Acta Materialia*, 114, 33–42. DOI: 10.1016/j.actamat.2016.05.017\\n2. Ly, S. et al. (2017). Metal vapor micro-jet controls material redistribution in laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing. *Scientific Reports*, 7, 4085. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-017-04237-z\\n3. Bidare, P. et al. (2018). Fluid and particle dynamics in laser powder bed fusion. *Acta Materialia*, 142, 107–120. DOI: 10.1016/j.actamat.2017.09.051\\n4. Yadroitsev, I. et al. (2010). Single track formation in selective laser melting of metal powders. *Journal of Materials Processing Technology*, 210, 1624–1631. DOI: 10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2010.05.010\\n5. Kamath, C. et al. (2014). Density of additively-manufactured, 316L SS parts using laser powder-bed fusion at powers up to 400 W. *International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology*, 74, 65–78. DOI: 10.1007/s00170-014-5954-9\\n6. Karayagiz, K. et al. (2019). Finite interface dissipation phase field modeling of Ni-Nb under additive manufacturing conditions. *Acta Materialia*, 185, 320–339. DOI: 10.1016/j.actamat.2019.12.014\\n7. Ladewig, A. et al. (2016). Influence of the shielding gas flow on the removal of process by-products in the selective laser melting process. *Additive Manufacturing*, 12, 307–319. DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2016.06.012\\n8. Gunenthiram, V. et al. (2018). Experimental analysis of spatter generation and melt-pool behavior during the powder bed laser beam melting process. *Journal of Materials Processing Technology*, 251, 376–386. DOI: 10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2017.08.012\\n9. Montgomery, C. et al. (2019). NIST AM Bench test series. *Integrating Materials and Manufacturing Innovation*, 8, 447–461. DOI: 10.1007/s40192-019-00155-y\\n10. Aboulkhair, N. T. et al. (2014). Reducing porosity in AlSi10Mg parts processed by selective laser melting. *Additive Manufacturing*, 1–4, 77–86. **Important note on sources:** All external literature retrieval services were unavailable during this analysis (paper search, patent search, and database tools returned zero results across all queries). The following answer is therefore compiled from established domain knowledge of the published literature. All references are cited by author, year, journal, and DOI; the reader should verify DOIs and specific numerical values against the original publications before finalizing experimental designs. No retrieved-document context IDs are available for citation.

---

## 1. Powder Denudation: Width, Mechanism, and Scaling

### Mechanism

At atmospheric pressure (1 atm Ar or N₂), the dominant denudation mechanism is vapour-jet-driven ambient-gas entrainment. The intense metal vapour plume rising from the melt pool entrains surrounding shielding gas, creating a low-pressure region near the substrate surface that draws gas and entrained powder particles inward toward the melt track. Particles are either incorporated into the melt pool or ejected upward as spatter.

Matthews et al. (2016, *Acta Materialia* 114, 33–42, DOI: 10.1016/j.actamat.2016.05.017) demonstrated using high-speed imaging that denudation at 1 atm in 316L and Ti-6Al-4V is driven by inward gas flow induced by the metal vapour jet. At reduced pressures (below ~1–10 Torr), the mechanism reverses and particles are blown outward.

Ly et al. (2017, *Scientific Reports* 7, 4085, DOI: 10.1038/s41598-017-04237-z) confirmed the mechanism with ultra-high-speed imaging, showing particles drawn toward the track at 1–10 m/s, and identified melt-pool-wetting capture as a secondary mechanism.

Bidare et al. (2018, *Acta Materialia* 142, 107–120, DOI: 10.1016/j.actamat.2017.09.051) systematically varied ambient pressure and confirmed the transition between mechanisms.

### Quantitative Denuded-Zone Widths

For 316L at P ≈ 150–200 W, v ≈ 0.5–1.5 m/s, ~50 µm spot, ~30–50 µm layer, 1 atm Ar: the total denuded zone (track + cleared region on both sides) is typically 2–5× the solidified track width. For track widths of ~100–200 µm, denudation extends ~100–400 µm beyond the track edge on each side. At higher power or lower speed (keyhole regime, P ≈ 300–400 W, v < 0.8 m/s), total denuded widths can reach 0.5–1.0 mm or more.

### Ratio of Denuded-Zone Width to Track Width

The ratio of total denuded-zone width to bead width is typically 2–5× at atmospheric pressure. This ratio increases with linear energy density (P/v) and is largest in keyhole conditions.

---

## 2. How a Previously Fused Neighbour Changes the Next Track

When a second track is placed within the first track's denuded zone, several effects arise: (a) reduced or absent powder on the near side, reducing available mass and creating asymmetric bead geometry; (b) the first track's raised solidified bead (typically 10–40 µm above the substrate for a single layer) altering local geometry and gas flow; (c) pre-captured particles unavailable to the second track; and (d) modest residual heat if exposed soon after.

Yadroitsev et al. (2010, *Journal of Materials Processing Technology* 210, 1624–1631, DOI: 10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2010.05.010) showed that decreasing hatch spacing below ~60–70% of single-track width degraded second-track geometry and promoted balling. Single-track stability maps change when neighbours are present. To ensure each track behaves as if isolated, centre-to-centre spacing must exceed the total denuded-zone width, practically ≥3× the expected melt-pool width (≥1.5–2.5 mm for typical 316L conditions).

---

## 3. Spatter and Ejecta

Spatter particles travel 1–20 mm, with most landing within 2–5 mm. Smaller particles carried by cross-flow gas can travel >10 mm downstream. In commercial machines like the Concept Laser M2, shielding gas flows at ~1–3 m/s across the build plate (Ladewig et al. 2016, *Additive Manufacturing* 12, 307–319, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2016.06.012).

The optimal exposure strategy is to expose tracks from the gas-outlet (downstream) side toward the gas-inlet (upstream) side, so that spatter and condensate are carried onto already-exposed regions. For scan direction, scanning into (against) the gas flow is preferred as the plume is blown away from the advancing melt pool, minimizing beam attenuation. Scanning with the gas flow prolongs plume-beam interaction.

The vapour plume attenuates the 1070 nm laser beam primarily by scattering from condensed nanoparticles. The magnitude depends on gas flow velocity and the scan direction relative to the flow.

---

## 4. Thermal Effects from Neighbouring Tracks

For 316L (thermal diffusivity α ≈ 4–5 mm²/s), the Rosenthal solution shows that at 1.5–2 mm lateral distance from a track centreline, the quasi-steady-state temperature rise is of order 1–10 °C for P = 200 W at v = 1 m/s. At ≥2.5 mm, the rise is negligible (<1–2 °C). After the laser passes, temperature decays rapidly; within ~0.1–1 s, temperatures at >1 mm are within a few degrees of ambient.

For single-layer tracks separated by ≥1.5–2 mm with ordinary galvo repositioning delays (~0.01–1 s), thermal pre-heating is negligible compared to melt-pool temperatures (~1400–1700 °C). Exposure order and waiting time are not critical for thermal reasons but remain important for denudation and spatter reasons.

---

## 5. Published Single-Track Study Practices

Key published practices include:

- Yadroitsev et al. (2010): 10–20 mm tracks, 1–3 mm spacing, 10–50+ tracks per panel, Phenix PM100, 50–70 W, 70 µm spot, 316L.
- Kamath et al. (2014, *IJAMT* 74, 65–78, DOI: 10.1007/s00170-014-5954-9): Concept Laser M2, 316L, 150–400 W, 0.1–2.2 m/s, 30 µm layer, ~2 mm spacing, 10 mm tracks, dozens per 80×80 mm substrate.
- NIST AM Bench (2018, 2022): IN625 and 316L, tracks 1–12 mm, spacing 1.25–4 mm (Montgomery et al. 2019, DOI: 10.1007/s40192-019-00155-y).
- Aboulkhair et al. (2014, *Additive Manufacturing* 1–4, 77–86, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2014.08.001): AlSi10Mg, ~10 mm tracks, several mm spacing.

For sectioning: precision saw kerf ~0.3–0.8 mm; 25–30 mm standard mounts fit 12–15 tracks at 2 mm spacing; SEM fields of 0.2–2 mm depending on magnification. Section 80 mm panels into 2–3 pieces for standard mounts.

---

## 6. The Effective Powder Layer

A single layer of 15–45 µm gas-atomized 316L powder has a packing fraction of ~50–65%, giving effective solid thickness t_eff = φ × t_nom ≈ 15–30 µm for 30–50 µm nominal layers. Substrate height offsets add directly to the actual layer thickness and can dominate melt-pool geometry. Target panel-to-plate alignment of ±5–10 µm.

The Thermo-Calc AM Module treats powder as a continuum with reduced thermal conductivity (~1–5% of bulk) and reduced density. Effective thickness and packing fraction are inputs; absorptivity is a calibration parameter. The Eagar–Tsai model does not explicitly model the powder layer; its effects are absorbed into calibrated absorptivity.

---

## Practical Recommendation Table

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### Confidence Summary

- **Strongly supported:** Denudation mechanism at 1 atm; qualitative scaling with P/v; downstream-to-upstream exposure; importance of scan direction vs. gas flow; effective powder layer < nominal.

# Isolating Single Tracks in Laser Powder Bed Fusion: Spacing, Exposure Order, and Practical Design

## 1. Powder Denudation: Width, Mechanism, and Scaling

**Mechanism.** At atmospheric pressure (1 atm Ar or N₂), the dominant denudation mechanism is vapour-jet-driven ambient-gas entrainment. The metal vapour plume rising from the melt pool entrains surrounding shielding gas, creating a low-pressure zone near the substrate that draws gas and powder particles inward toward the melt track. Particles are either incorporated into the melt pool or ejected upward as spatter. This was demonstrated by Matthews et al. (2016, *Acta Materialia* 114, 33–42, DOI: 10.1016/j.actamat.2016.05.017) using high-speed imaging in 316L SS and Ti-6Al-4V. At reduced pressures (<1–10 Torr), the mechanism reverses: expanding vapour directly ejects particles outward, creating an even wider denuded zone. Ly et al. (2017, *Scientific Reports* 7, 4085, DOI: 10.1038/s41598-017-04237-z) confirmed the entrainment mechanism and identified melt-pool-wetting capture as a secondary mechanism. Bidare et al. (2018, *Acta Materialia* 142, 107–120, DOI: 10.1016/j.actamat.2017.09.051) systematically varied pressure (0.01–1000 mbar Ar) and confirmed the mechanism transition.

**Quantitative widths.** For 316L at P≈150–200 W, v≈0.5–1.5 m/s, ~50 µm spot, 30–50 µm layer, 1 atm Ar: the total denuded zone (track plus cleared regions on both sides) is typically 2–5× the solidified track width. For track widths ~100–200 µm, denudation extends ~100–400 µm beyond the track edge on each side (Matthews et al. 2016; Ly et al. 2017). At higher power or lower speed (keyhole regime, P≈300–400 W, v<0.8 m/s), total denuded widths reach 0.5–1.0 mm or more. In Ti-6Al-4V, denudation is similar or somewhat larger. In AlSi10Mg, denudation can be particularly wide due to the high vapour pressure of Mg (Yin et al. 2020, *Additive Manufacturing* 31, 100958, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2019.100958). The ratio of total denuded-zone width to track width is 2–5× at atmospheric pressure and increases with linear energy density (P/v).

## 2. How a Previously Fused Neighbour Changes the Next Track

When a second track is placed within the first track's denuded zone, several effects alter the second track: (a) reduced or absent powder on the near side creates asymmetric bead geometry with reduced height; (b) the first track's raised solidified bead (10–40 µm above substrate) alters local geometry and gas flow; (c) particles previously captured by the first track's melt pool are unavailable; (d) modest residual heat if exposed soon after. Yadroitsev et al. (2010, *J. Materials Processing Technology* 210, 1624–1631, DOI: 10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2010.05.010) showed that hatch spacing below ~60–70% of single-track width degrades second-track geometry and promotes balling. To ensure isolation, centre-to-centre spacing must exceed the total denuded-zone width, practically ≥3× the expected melt-pool width, or ≥1.5–2.5 mm for typical 316L conditions.

## 3. Spatter and Ejecta

Spatter particles travel 1–20 mm from the scan track, with most landing within 2–5 mm. Smaller particles carried by cross-flow shielding gas can travel >10 mm downstream. In commercial L-PBF machines like the Concept Laser M2, shielding gas flows at approximately 1–3 m/s across the build plate (Ladewig et al. 2016, *Additive Manufacturing* 12, 307–319, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2016.06.012). The optimal exposure strategy is to expose tracks progressively from the gas-outlet (downstream) side toward the gas-inlet (upstream) side, so that spatter and condensate are carried onto already-exposed regions rather than contaminating remaining powder. For scan direction, scanning into (against) the gas flow is preferred as the plume is blown away from the advancing melt pool, minimizing beam attenuation by condensed nanoparticles in the plume.

## 4. Thermal Effects from Neighbouring Tracks

For 316L (thermal diffusivity α ≈ 4–5 mm²/s), the Rosenthal solution gives a quasi-steady-state temperature rise at 1.5–2 mm lateral distance of order 1–10°C for P = 200 W, v = 1 m/s. At ≥2.5 mm, the rise is <1–2°C. Within 0.1–1 s after the laser passes, temperatures at >1 mm are within a few degrees of ambient. For single-layer isolated tracks separated by ≥1.5–2 mm on a thick substrate with galvo delays (~0.01–1 s), thermal effects are negligible compared to melt-pool temperatures (~1400–1700°C). Exposure order matters for denudation and spatter reasons, not thermal reasons.

The Thermo-Calc AM Module models powder as a continuum with reduced conductivity (~1–5% of bulk) and reduced density; packing fraction and thickness are inputs, absorptivity is calibrated. 1. # Isolating Single Tracks in Laser Powder Bed Fusion: Spacing, Exposure Order, and Practical Design

## 1. Powder Denudation: Width, Mechanism, and Scaling

**Mechanism.** At atmospheric pressure (1 atm Ar or N₂), the dominant denudation mechanism is vapour-jet-driven ambient-gas entrainment. The metal vapour plume rising from the melt pool entrains surrounding shielding gas, creating a low-pressure zone near the substrate that draws gas and powder particles inward toward the melt track. Particles are either incorporated into the melt pool or ejected upward as spatter. This was demonstrated by Matthews et al. (2016, *Acta Materialia* 114, 33–42, DOI: 10.1016/j.actamat.2016.05.017) using high-speed imaging in 316L SS and Ti-6Al-4V. At reduced pressures (<1–10 Torr), the mechanism reverses: expanding vapour directly ejects particles outward, creating an even wider denuded zone. Ly et al. (2017, *Scientific Reports* 7, 4085, DOI: 10.1038/s41598-017-04237-z) confirmed the entrainment mechanism and identified melt-pool-wetting capture as a secondary mechanism. Bidare et al. (2018, *Acta Materialia* 142, 107–120, DOI: 10.1016/j.actamat.2017.09.051) systematically varied pressure (0.01–1000 mbar Ar) and confirmed the mechanism transition.

**Quantitative widths.** For 316L at P≈150–200 W, v≈0.5–1.5 m/s, ~50 µm spot, 30–50 µm layer, 1 atm Ar: the total denuded zone (track plus cleared regions on both sides) is typically 2–5× the solidified track width. For track widths ~100–200 µm, denudation extends ~100–400 µm beyond the track edge on each side (Matthews et al. 2016; Ly et al. 2017). At higher power or lower speed (keyhole regime, P≈300–400 W, v<0.8 m/s), total denuded widths reach 0.5–1.0 mm or more. In Ti-6Al-4V, denudation is similar or somewhat larger. In AlSi10Mg, denudation can be particularly wide due to the high vapour pressure of Mg (Yin et al. 2020, *Additive Manufacturing* 31, 100958, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2019.100958). The ratio of total denuded-zone width to track width is 2–5× at atmospheric pressure and increases with linear energy density (P/v).

## 2. How a Previously Fused Neighbour Changes the Next Track

When a second track is placed within the first track's denuded zone, several effects alter the second track: (a) reduced or absent powder on the near side creates asymmetric bead geometry with reduced height; (b) the first track's raised solidified bead (10–40 µm above substrate) alters local geometry and gas flow; (c) particles previously captured by the first track's melt pool are unavailable; (d) modest residual heat if exposed soon after. Yadroitsev et al. (2010, *J. Materials Processing Technology* 210, 1624–1631, DOI: 10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2010.05.010) showed that hatch spacing below ~60–70% of single-track width degrades second-track geometry and promotes balling. To ensure isolation, centre-to-centre spacing must exceed the total denuded-zone width, practically ≥3× the expected melt-pool width, or ≥1.5–2.5 mm for typical 316L conditions.

## 3. Spatter and Ejecta

Spatter particles travel 1–20 mm from the scan track, with most landing within 2–5 mm. Smaller particles carried by cross-flow shielding gas can travel >10 mm downstream. In commercial L-PBF machines like the Concept Laser M2, shielding gas flows at approximately 1–3 m/s across the build plate (Ladewig et al. 2016, *Additive Manufacturing* 12, 307–319, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2016.06.012). The optimal exposure strategy is to expose tracks progressively from the gas-outlet (downstream) side toward the gas-inlet (upstream) side, so that spatter and condensate are carried onto already-exposed regions rather than contaminating remaining powder. For scan direction, scanning into (against) the gas flow is preferred as the plume is blown away from the advancing melt pool, minimizing beam attenuation by condensed nanoparticles in the plume.

## 4. Thermal Effects from Neighbouring Tracks

For 316L (thermal diffusivity α ≈ 4–5 mm²/s), the Rosenthal solution gives a quasi-steady-state temperature rise at 1.5–2 mm lateral distance of order 1–10°C for P = 200 W, v = 1 m/s. At ≥2.5 mm, the rise is <1–2°C. Within 0.1–1 s after the laser passes, temperatures at >1 mm are within a few degrees of ambient. For single-layer isolated tracks separated by ≥1.5–2 mm on a thick substrate with galvo delays (~0.01–1 s), thermal effects are negligible compared to melt-pool temperatures (~1400–1700°C). Exposure order matters for denudation and spatter reasons, not thermal reasons.

## 5. Published Single-Track Study Practices

Key practices: Yadroitsev et al. (2010): 10–20 mm tracks, 1–3 mm spacing, Phenix PM100, 50–70 W, 70 µm spot. Kamath et al. (2014, *IJAMT* 74, 65–78, DOI: 10.1007/s00170-014-5954-9): Concept Laser M2, 316L, 150–400 W, 30 µm layer, ~2 mm spacing, 10 mm tracks, dozens per 80 mm substrate. NIST AM Bench (2018, 2022): IN625 and 316L, tracks 1–12 mm, spacing 1.25–4 mm (Montgomery et al. 2019, DOI: 10.1007/s40192-019-00155-y). Sectioning: precision saw kerf ~0.3–0.8 mm; 25–30 mm mounts fit 12–15 tracks at 2 mm spacing.

## 6. The Effective Powder Layer

Packing fraction of spread 15–45 µm 316L powder is ~50–65%, giving effective solid thickness t_eff ≈ 15–30 µm for 30–50 µm nominal layers. Substrate height offsets add directly. The Thermo-Calc AM Module models powder as a continuum with reduced conductivity (~1–5% of bulk) and reduced density; packing fraction and thickness are inputs, absorptivity is calibrated. The Eagar–Tsai model does not explicitly model the powder layer.

|---|---|---|---|

Denudation can extend several track half-widths from the centreline; its exact extent varies with power, speed, layer thickness, pressure, and keyholing. A short sacrificial pilot row should verify that undisturbed powder remains midway between tracks. | **Strong** for conservative isolation; **Moderate** for the exact denudation scaling, especially in high-power keyhole conditions. |
| Exposure order | Expose tracks progressively from the **gas-outlet/downstream side toward the gas-inlet/upstream side**. | With gas flowing inlet → outlet, plume condensate and entrained ejecta are carried toward already exposed positions rather than across powder reserved for later tracks. Confirm actual flow direction at plate height rather than relying only on machine labels. | **Strong** for the downstream-to-upstream principle where cross-flow is uniform. |
| Scan direction relative to gas flow | Prefer vectors scanned **into the gas flow** or **across it**; avoid scanning in the same direction as the gas flow unless a machine-specific trial shows no degradation. Keep direction identical across calibration and validation tracks, or balance directions as an explicit experimental factor. | Opposing or transverse motion generally promotes plume removal from the beam–melt-pool interaction region; co-flow scanning can prolong beam–plume interaction and deposit ejecta farther along the unexposed vector. Machine-specific flow nonuniformity can alter the result. | **Strong** for controlling and reporting orientation; **Moderate** for a universal ranking of into-flow versus cross-flow. |
| Position randomization | Do **not** expose geometrically adjacent tracks consecutively. Use an interleaved sequence such as odd positions followed by even positions, while retaining the overall outlet-to-inlet progression; randomize process-condition assignment within compatible spatial blocks. | Interleaving increases spatial separation and elapsed time between neighbouring exposures, reducing correlated thermal history, local powder depletion, and contamination. Unrestricted randomization can defeat the outlet-to-inlet contamination strategy, so use constrained randomization. | **Moderate**. |
| Track length | Use **10–15 mm** vectors. Place the transverse measurement plane at least **5 mm after the start** and preferably **≥3–5 mm before the end**. | Excludes acceleration, turn-on, initial melt-pool growth, and laser turn-off effects and better approximates the steady travelling-source assumption used by Thermo-Calc and Eagar–Tsai calculations. | **Moderate–Strong**. |
| Margin from panel edges | Keep track centrelines and the section plane **≥3 mm** from a free panel edge; use **≥5 mm** where space permits. Keep starts and stops away from insert joints, bolt regions, height steps, and recoater-disturbed margins. | Reduces free-edge heat-flow effects, powder-thickness changes, local gas-flow disturbances, and mechanical/flatness effects associated with the removable panel. The conservative margin should exceed both the denudation scale and the near-field thermal scale. | **Moderate**. |
| Waiting time between tracks | Ordinary galvanometer repositioning of approximately **0.1–1 s** is generally adequate when tracks are separated by **1.5–2.5 mm** and interleaved. Use multiple rows only if their separation and sectioning plan preserve the same isolation criteria. | The usable width is roughly 74 mm: inclusive endpoint counting gives approximately floor(74/pitch)+1 positions. Final capacity also depends on saw kerf, mount diameter, labels, bolt locations, and the need to keep every measured cross-section in one polished plane. | **Strong** for geometry; **Moderate** for practical capacity. |


*Table: Practical layout and exposure recommendations for isolated 316L single tracks at 50–400 W, 0.1–3 m/s, 30–50 µm nominal layer thickness, and 1 atm Ar or N₂. Confidence labels distinguish robust isolation principles from machine-dependent numerical thresholds.*

**Confidence summary:** Strongly supported: denudation mechanism at 1 atm; downstream-to-upstream exposure; scan direction vs gas flow. Moderately supported: specific denudation widths; thermal thresholds; packing fractions. Weakly supported: exact thermal thresholds; precise spatter distances; universal spacing values.

# Isolating Single Tracks in Laser Powder Bed Fusion: Spacing, Exposure Order, and Practical Design

## 1. Powder Denudation: Width, Mechanism, and Scaling

**Mechanism.** At atmospheric pressure (1 atm Ar or N₂), the dominant denudation mechanism is vapour-jet-driven ambient-gas entrainment. The metal vapour plume rising from the melt pool entrains surrounding shielding gas, creating a low-pressure zone near the substrate that draws gas and powder particles inward toward the melt track. Particles are either incorporated into the melt pool or ejected upward as spatter. This was demonstrated by Matthews et al. (2016, *Acta Materialia* 114, 33–42, DOI: 10.1016/j.actamat.2016.05.017) using high-speed imaging in 316L SS and Ti-6Al-4V. At reduced pressures (<1–10 Torr), the mechanism reverses: expanding vapour directly ejects particles outward, creating an even wider denuded zone. Ly et al. (2017, *Scientific Reports* 7, 4085, DOI: 10.1038/s41598-017-04237-z) confirmed the entrainment mechanism and identified melt-pool-wetting capture as a secondary mechanism. Bidare et al. (2018, *Acta Materialia* 142, 107–120, DOI: 10.1016/j.actamat.2017.09.051) systematically varied pressure (0.01–1000 mbar Ar) and confirmed the mechanism transition.

**Quantitative widths.** For 316L at P≈150–200 W, v≈0.5–1.5 m/s, ~50 µm spot, 30–50 µm layer, 1 atm Ar: the total denuded zone (track plus cleared regions on both sides) is typically 2–5× the solidified track width. For track widths ~100–200 µm, denudation extends ~100–400 µm beyond the track edge on each side (Matthews et al. 2016; Ly et al. 2017). At higher power or lower speed (keyhole regime, P≈300–400 W, v<0.8 m/s), total denuded widths reach 0.5–1.0 mm or more. In Ti-6Al-4V, denudation is similar or somewhat larger. In AlSi10Mg, denudation can be particularly wide due to the high vapour pressure of Mg (Yin et al. 2020, *Additive Manufacturing* 31, 100958, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2019.100958). The ratio of total denuded-zone width to track width is 2–5× at atmospheric pressure and increases with linear energy density (P/v).

## 2. How a Previously Fused Neighbour Changes the Next Track

When a second track is placed within the first track's denuded zone, several effects alter the second track: (a) reduced or absent powder on the near side creates asymmetric bead geometry with reduced height; (b) the first track's raised solidified bead (10–40 µm above substrate) alters local geometry and gas flow; (c) particles previously captured by the first track's melt pool are unavailable; (d) modest residual heat if exposed soon after. Yadroitsev et al. (2010, *J. Materials Processing Technology* 210, 1624–1631, DOI: 10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2010.05.010) showed that hatch spacing below ~60–70% of single-track width degrades second-track geometry and promotes balling. To ensure isolation, centre-to-centre spacing must exceed the total denuded-zone width, practically ≥3× the expected melt-pool width, or ≥1.5–2.5 mm for typical 316L conditions.

## 3. Spatter and Ejecta

Spatter particles travel 1–20 mm from the scan track, with most landing within 2–5 mm. Smaller particles carried by cross-flow shielding gas can travel >10 mm downstream. In commercial L-PBF machines like the Concept Laser M2, shielding gas flows at approximately 1–3 m/s across the build plate (Ladewig et al. 2016, *Additive Manufacturing* 12, 307–319, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2016.06.012). The optimal exposure strategy is to expose tracks progressively from the gas-outlet (downstream) side toward the gas-inlet (upstream) side, so that spatter and condensate are carried onto already-exposed regions rather than contaminating remaining powder. For scan direction, scanning into (against) the gas flow is preferred as the plume is blown away from the advancing melt pool, minimizing beam attenuation by condensed nanoparticles in the plume.

## 4. Thermal Effects from Neighbouring Tracks

For 316L (thermal diffusivity α ≈ 4–5 mm²/s), the Rosenthal solution gives a quasi-steady-state temperature rise at 1.5–2 mm lateral distance of order 1–10°C for P = 200 W, v = 1 m/s. At ≥2.5 mm, the rise is <1–2°C. Within 0.1–1 s after the laser passes, temperatures at >1 mm are within a few degrees of ambient. For single-layer isolated tracks separated by ≥1.5–2 mm on a thick substrate with galvo delays (~0.01–1 s), thermal effects are negligible compared to melt-pool temperatures (~1400–1700°C). Exposure order matters for denudation and spatter reasons, not thermal reasons.

## 5. Published Single-Track Study Practices

Key practices: Yadroitsev et al. (2010): 10–20 mm tracks, 1–3 mm spacing, Phenix PM100, 50–70 W, 70 µm spot. Kamath et al. (2014, *IJAMT* 74, 65–78, DOI: 10.1007/s00170-014-5954-9): Concept Laser M2, 316L, 150–400 W, 30 µm layer, ~2 mm spacing, 10 mm tracks, dozens per 80 mm substrate. NIST AM Bench (2018, 2022): IN625 and 316L, tracks 1–12 mm, spacing 1.25–4 mm (Montgomery et al. 2019, DOI: 10.1007/s40192-019-00155-y). Sectioning: precision saw kerf ~0.3–0.8 mm; 25–30 mm mounts fit 12–15 tracks at 2 mm spacing.

## 6. The Effective Powder Layer

Packing fraction of spread 15–45 µm 316L powder is ~50–65%, giving effective solid thickness t_eff ≈ 15–30 µm for 30–50 µm nominal layers. Substrate height offsets add directly. The Thermo-Calc AM Module models powder as a continuum with reduced conductivity (~1–5% of bulk) and reduced density; packing fraction and thickness are inputs, absorptivity is calibrated. The Eagar–Tsai model does not explicitly model the powder layer.

|---|---|---|---|
| Minimum centre-to-centre track spacing | Use **≥1.5 mm** routinely and **2.0–2.5 mm** for the highest-power, slowest, keyhole-prone conditions. Also require spacing to exceed **3× the measured melt-pool width**; apply whichever criterion is larger. | Prevent overlap with the neighbour’s powder-denuded zone. Denudation can extend several track half-widths from the centreline; its exact extent varies with power, speed, layer thickness, pressure, and keyholing. A short sacrificial pilot row should verify that undisturbed powder remains midway between tracks. | **Strong** for conservative isolation; **Moderate** for the exact denudation scaling, especially in high-power keyhole conditions. |

Keep direction identical across calibration and validation tracks, or balance directions as an explicit experimental factor. | Opposing or transverse motion generally promotes plume removal from the beam–melt-pool interaction region; co-flow scanning can prolong beam–plume interaction and deposit ejecta farther along the unexposed vector. Machine-specific flow nonuniformity can alter the result. | **Strong** for controlling and reporting orientation; **Moderate** for a universal ranking of into-flow versus cross-flow. |

Keep starts and stops away from insert joints, bolt regions, height steps, and recoater-disturbed margins. | Reduces free-edge heat-flow effects, powder-thickness changes, local gas-flow disturbances, and mechanical/flatness effects associated with the removable panel.
